not going to impugn the motives of the Minister of Railways in making this motion-that Bills are sent to the Railway Committee for the purpose of being slaughtered. I do not think that is his intention. He has stated his intention, and I must give him credit for being perfectly fair in the matter. The Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance or the Minister^ of Railways in introducing a Bill dealing with matters connected with his department, does not think of sending that Bill to one of the committees of this House. This seems to be a new departure, and there must be something behind it. I think that the old procedure is the better one. There is no reason, to my mind, why this parliament should go beyond this House for aid in this matter. If there is, then it should be plainly stated, and the House should be convinced that its jurisdiction is not sufficient, that somebody else must be called in to give advice to parliament on the simple matter of what a layman's rights are in this court, whether they are to be clear, or whether they are to remain uncertain for ten, twenty or thirty years, and that he is always to stand in jeopardy of what might be sprung upon him some day without notice. I hope the House will consent to deal with the Bill at once, to put it through committee, if it is believed to be a fair Bill, and give the laymen of this country that protection to which they are entitled, without any technical attempt being made to destroy the legislation which the hon. gentleman is trying to get passed.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. LANCASTER moved the second reading of Bill (No. 4) to amend the Railway Act, he said: This Bill, as I explained, on the first reading, is to correct what I think is a manifest injustice arising out of the amendments made to the Railway Act last year. When I was introducing the Bill I understood the Minister of Railways to say that he considered it an interference with the principle that had been adopted by this House last session in regard to his amendments. I wish to say that I think the hon. gentleman misapprehends the Bill entirely, though it may have been my fault in not sufficiently explaining the Bill. I understood the hon. gentleman then to say that I was violating the principle which he had got the House to adopt last year, namely, that there should be a contribution from the railways, the municipalities and the Dominion government to protect all crossings where highways are crossed by railways. But the section which I propose to amend here does not deal with that, but with the exceptions the hon. gentleman put through the House last session in regard to that matter. The section I propose to amend is Mr. HENDERSON.
the very opposite of what the hon. gentleman had in his mind when I introduced the Bill. I will read the legislation passed by this House last year on this question, which is to be found in chapter 32 of the Acts of last session.
238a. In any case where a railway is constructed after the passing of this Act, the company shall, at its own cost and expense (unless and except as otherwise provided by agreement, approved of by the board, between the company and a municipal or other corporation or person), provide, subject to the order of the board, all protection, safety and convenience for the public in respect of any crossing of a highway by the railway.
That is the section of the Act I am amending, and that section puts the whole cost upon the railway if it is a railway that is constructed after the passing of that Act. ' The Bill is now printed, and by it I am seeking to amend that section by adding these words:
And where the railway has been constructed before the passing of this Act,

The converse of the case put by the hon. gentleman in his section last session.
-and is permitted by the board to pass over any highway crossing at rail level, the municipality shall not be ordered to pay any portion of the cost or expense of protecting such crossing unless and except it is otherwise provided by agreement, approved of by the board, between the company and the municipal corporation.
As the law stands to-day, a railway that is incorporated since last session has to bear the whole expense of protecting these crossings, no matter how well they may protect it, no matter what they may do in the shape of bridging or subterranean passages, no matter what works the board may order them to do, no matter how ideal the protection may be which they afford, they have to pay the whole expense if their railway was constructed after the passing of this Act of last session. Now, I am not saying that it is not always right to discriminate between railways, but we are certainly making a great discrimination here. We are saying that any railway that wishes to come into competition with the railways that were in operation last session shall have it up against them to bear the enormous expense of protecting a crossing, an expense to which neither the Dominion nor the municipality contributes, and no matter how good a protection they may afford. That is further than I would have gone, although I have been accused of being a radical in these matters. I would not have said that any corporation must do something that other rail-ways constructed before it did not have to do. That is a discrimination against the later railway, and is calculated to discourage the construction of competing railways. But

when we say that railways which are constructed since the passing of the Act of last session must, no matter what ideal condition they may create for the perfect safety of the people, pay all the expenses of such protection, and that the hoard has no power to apportion those expenses upon anybody else, we should at least say that where these old railways which are using the King's highway refuse to create the ideal condition which the board might order them to create, or object to doing so, in that case we should at least say that no portion of such protection as the board finds necessary over a dangerous crossing, should be borne by the municipality. I never could see why they should. The 'board will order such contribution if we put the principle up to them, they will not order it if we say that the proper principle prevents them from doing so. Now, what should we do? I think that when we find the board going wrong wre should step in and set them right. We are here to see that the Board of Railway Commissioners does what we think the people want them to do, and that they properly administer the affairs that we send to them to be administered.
The board holds as a matter of course, that the municipality shall always contribute. They are entitled to hold that. I am not finding fault with their power. If they choose to do so, they have the power to so hold unless you say, as a parliament, that there must be a distinction made. The Minister of Railways and Canals made the distinction last session in the law which I am now seeking to amend and he said that the board shall not be allowed to put upon the municipal or the Dominion fund, which was created for the purpose, any portion of the expense for protecting any highway from danger by a railway if the railway was not constructed before last year. But, these are not the railways that we are dealing with They do not exist. They are not killing peo-T.de because they are not being operated. They are only in people's minds at the present time. There is no harm being done by them. They have not been constructed yet and they are unable to hurt anybody because they do not exist. But, we have before us the condition of affairs in which the railways that were constructed before last session of this parliament continue to kill people upon highway crossings where the highway and the railway track are upon the same level, and you cannot go upon the highway without running the risk of being hit by a train. Who creates the danger? What principle are you going to go by? There is the danger in running across the King's highway. They are persisting in running their trains across the highway instead of protecting the crossing, persisting in saying that they do not think it fair to
require them to erect overhead or underground structures so that they cannot hit anybody because it will cost a lot of money and persisting in saying that they are going to run across the highway and create the danger rather than incur the expense which the commission may think they ought to incur in creating a better condition. The first question that we must ask is: Who creates the danger? It is the railway. I have heard it said-I never heard the Railway Commission decide it myself-but I have heard it said that the Railway Commissioners have said that they think that the public should help to protect these crossings because the public helned to create the danger. If that is the position of the Railway Commission, I think that parliament should condemn it. It is said that if a man owning a piece of property which the railway company did not expropriate erects a building upon that land which obscures the view of the railway he is doing something to create a danger and that therefore he and the municipality in which he lives should contribute towards the protection oi the crossing. He has a perfect right to build upon his own land. The fact that the railway runs near it is no reason why he should not build upon that land if he wants to. I understand the commission holds that because he does construct that building which may obscure a view of the railway he and the municipality should contribute towards the protection of the crossing. That is confiscation. We have heard hon. gentlemen on behalf of the railway companies in this House-hon. gentlemen who might be trying to do their duty in the public interest-speaking of confiscation. Might not this be said to be confiscation of a private owner's property? You are putting a limitation upon his right of ownership. The railways say to him: If you erect a building upon your own land near the railway track which may obscure a view of the train coming down to this level crossing, you are helping us to create a dangerous condition there and, although we are the ones who run the trains and kill the people, you have placed your building so that they cannot see our track or the danger and you must tear your building down or you and the municipality in which you live must pay a tax to create a fund for the purpose of protecting that crossing. These are the special arguments put forward by the railways before the commission, more or less appealing to the commission, but when you scan them vou find that there is no merit in them. The man who owns land outside of railway control has a perfect right to build upon it as much as he would if he were ten miles away, and he should not be prevented from building because he is going to be accused of obscuring the level crossing and the train coming down the

track to it. Now, the danger is entirely created by the railway and the protection should be at their expense as long as they persist in running upon the highway.
There is another question involved here and some fine day somebody, will find it out, at a good deal of expense and disappointment perhaps to those concerned. I do not believe that this House, or, at all events, the government, in passing this legislation last year, gave anything }ike the consideration it shoul'd have had to what their power is to say that municipalities shall pay the cost of protecting the highway crossings assessed by a Dominion board. When had this parliament power to create any board to tax any municipality? Under the British North America Act who does control municipal government? Where did parliament ever get and how has it any vires or right whatever to deal with this question of municipalities protecting highway crossings under the orders of a creature created entirely by the Dominion parliament and having nothing whatever to do with the local legislatures which have the power to tax for municipal purposes? You are asking your board to say that the municipalities must contribute a certain proportion of the cost of protection of their own crossings which costs are to be put upon them by the Board of Railway Commissioners un'der the authority of a Dominion Act of parliament. You will find it some day decided, I am satisfied, that you have no power to do anything of the kind, and if a municipality against whom the board levied laughed in the face of the chairman and said: Go on and let us see, you collect this tax for crossings, the Board of Railway Commissioners could not collect it. They cannot do anything about it. If you bring an action how are you going to collect the tax? Who is going to impose the tax? Who is going to levy the assessment? This Dominion parliament cannot enforce the payment of anything of the sort unless perhaps they brought suit in the Exchequer Court against a municipality and seized a safe or a road roller. They cannot collect damages whatever they might be unless they could find some loose property of that kind that perhaps they might seize upon. You have not the power to levy any taxation upon any municipality for any such purpose and the right of the matter is probably as consistent as the right generally is with regard to technical powers. The reason that you were not given power by the framers of the British North America Act was because of the very great injustice of your attempting to exercise such a right. The municipalities control the highways, the highways are built by the municipalities with the aid of taxation levied by themselves, they are kept in repair for the convenience of the business of the country and if a railway crosses a highway upon a Mr. LANCASTER.
rail level and this Board of Railway Commissioners undertake to say that the municipality must pay a part of the tax it is a matter ultra vires of this parliament and besides that it is unmeritorious and not fair that it should be done.
The highways belong to the Crown.

The highways, as the hon. gentleman says, are the property of the Crown and are administered under the provincial legislatures. The provincial legislatures control the highways, they have passed this control on to the municipalities, the Dominion parliament has no power to tax the municipalities for anything done upon the highways and some day they will learn it to their cost. Orders made by the Railway Commission will have to be upset and you will have all sorts of confusion in regard to it.
But, the merits of the matter, outside of the technical question as to whether we are ultra or intra vires in passing such legislation is what appeals to me. Here is a railway constructed since last session trying to get into competition for the good of the country with railways that were constructed before last session and it is required to pay the whole expense. Not only is the municipality not to be charged but the Dominion fund is not to be drawn upon. But the railways which have done the harm, the railways that were constructed before last year, the railways that refused to protect these crossings, if the Board of Railway Commissioners find it necessary to protect them, are to be allowed to pay a portion of the expense only while they are running upon the highway and the municipality is to be ordered to pay part of the expense also. The effect of my proposed legislation is that where they do insist upon running upon the King's highway where they are likely to come in contact with people upon that highway the municipality must not be ordered to pay any portion of the cost. The board shall not have power to order them to unless they agree to it by some agreement which the board may sanction as fair and reasonable. That means that they cannot tax them without their consent. The board can still appropriate part of the Dominion fund to assist the railway, but they must keep their hands off the municipalities so long as the highways are being used by the railways for their own purposes. I move the second reading.

This is a very important and a somewhat large question, but as I discussed the matter fully last session, and as when certain statistics I have asked for are brought down I shall direct my attention to it again, I do not purpose going very fully in to the question now. I entirely agree with the object my hon. friend

(Mr. Lancaster) has in view and with the principle that underlies his Bill, and I want to add that the only objection I have to his Bill is that it does not go far enough.
Take what you can get.	-

It is well enough to take what we can get, but I have not very much faith that we will get anything this session, I prophesy, however, that sooner or later the minister will have to adopt the principle which this Bill propounds. What I contended last session and what I repeat this session is, that wherever a railway sees fit-whether it is a new railway or an old railway-to occupy a highway, then there should be no public contribution for protection. If the railway will increase the public safety by separating its line from the highway then I am in favour, under certain circumstances, of making contribution at the public expense. But in absolutely no case-whether it is the case of an existing railway or a new railway- am L in favour of giving one dollar out of the funds of the Dominion, and much less out of the funds of the municipalities, towards the construction of safety appliances so long as the railway endangers the public safety by occupying the public highway. The legislation passed by the minister last session was a step in the right direction and a fairly good step, but I then called his attention to the fact and that he should limit the assistance to cases in which the separation of the railway grade from the highway is effected. At first we understood that the minister would adopt that suggestion. Afterwards it was intimated that, at the suggestion of the chairman of the railway board, the minister concluded that he would allow the public funds to be diverted not only in the case of separation of highwavs from railways, but in the case of the erection of simple appliances such as gates, or bells, or other devices which afforded some remedy but not an adequate one. If the minister had confined the contribution of the public money to cases in which the railway company agreed to absolutely separate the railway from the highway then a great benefit to the public would have accrued and we would have had an incentive to the railway companies to pursue that course; but as it is, the public funds are contributed to the railway when they agree to erect some temporary appliance which does not afford a complete	remedy, and against	tha+ 1protest.	I	have	great pleasure	in supporting	the	Bill	introduced by	my hon.friend,	and I	hope it will	not be
very long before we will have legislation which will have the effect of saving not only the municipalities from having to contribute but which will prevent any contribution of any public moneys, to any purpose other than the separation of grades. There is absolutely no justification for contributing one dollar of the public funds, whether of the municipality or of the Dominion government, unless the railway separates the grades and thus for ever removes the danger to the public. I have asked certain information to be brought down on this matter. It is a question which will bear discussion from time to time. I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) with his usual energy and his great interest in questions which are for the benefit of the public has brought the matter forward. I hope he shall pursue his course until we at last attain to better conditions with regard to the crossings of highways by railways. '

There are hundreds of railway crossings in Canada the separation of which from the level is impracticable, and in respect to which the public can be well protected by a gate or some other device. And, if the public is protected then the object we all have in view is attained and there is no need for discussing technicalities. My hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) forgets that the chief expense is not in the construction of a gate but in its maintenance afterwards, and no part of the government fund goes towards that maintenance.
But the municipality has to pay.

I should think that if our object is the protection of the public then so long as the public are protected it makes no difference how that end is attained whether it is by the erection of a gate, or of a subway or of an overhead crossing. Now, the innocent way in which my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) words his clause will compel me to read this subsection to the House: He told us that he was amending subsection 238A, but it would occur to me as a layman that in amending 238A my hon. friend is amending the whole legislation of last session, although if one had not the Act before him his Bill would not appear to mean so much as it really does. Now let me read subsection of 238A, and apply it to the Bill:	.
Notwithstanding anything in this Act, the board may, subject to the provisions of sec. 238a, &c.
When you amend sec. 238a, you amend the whole power of the board.
That is what I intend.

This interferes with the principle of the Act passed last year. At that time we had a good deal of discussion on the question of why the municipalities or the government should participate at all. I could argue as strongly against the government participating as my hon. friend does against the municipalities participat-

ing. The argument, which has prevailed in the various states of the union, which prevailed in this House last year, and against which I have not heard one note of objection from a municipality in the province of Ontario, or arfywhere else, was this, that conditions now exist which did not exist in the early days of railway building. There must come a time when the line of demarcation must be drawn between existing roads and roads which are to come into existence. That line we drew last year, and the argument for it was this. In the early days of railway building, every municipality was so anxious to have a railway that it was willing to give railways level crossings wherever they liked to have them without restriction, property for stations and terminals and often large bonuses. The country was anxious to have railways, and the crossings were not supervised as they are now. The railway companies were building in a new country and had to do all the experimenting as to whether the lines would pay or not. There were three parties contributing-the railway company itself, the government, in not more closely scrutinizing, and the municipalities, in giving the railway companies any privileges they wanted. These three parties contributed to the establishment of level crossings all over the country. When a measure was proposed for the purpose of getting rid of the danger of level crossings, it was argued that the three parties who had contributed to -tins state of affairs might reasonably be asked to contribute in a proper measure to the removal of the evil. Now, Canada is not alone in that. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), who has given this matter a great deal of attention, knows that in the various states of the union the municipalities are asked to contribute, and to contribute very largely, and the larger municipalities are always prepared to do so.
They have always a fixed rate.
The rate fixed by the commission has been very small; but that does not interfere with my argument. The hon. member for Lincoln contends that municipalities should not be asked to contribute at all.
When the railway runs on the highway.

His argument was that municipalities should not be asked to pay at all. I am pointing out that every state in the union that has dealt with this question has asked the municipalities to contribute a certain amount, which is usually specified, but a comparatively small amount; but the principle has been accepted that the municipalities should be asked to contribute something. Now, I am not Mr. GRAHAM.
prepared to argue the legal point, but I have been told by eminent legal gentlemen that although an Act might apparently be beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament, or that of any provincial legislature, anything that is incidental to the enforcing of that Act comes within the jurisdiction of this parliament or of the legislature, as the case may be. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) stated that very clearly last session, giving as his authority the late Sir John Thompson. I have it on fairly good legal authority that the parliament of Canada can enforce against a municipality anything that it can enforce against an individual. But my hon. friend should not raise that point, because, if his argument be sound, he disposed of his apprehensions about our taxing municipalities. If we cannot tax municipalities, then his Bill would not be at all necessary, because we could not get anything out of them.

Did not the hon. gentleman understand me to say that there were two objections-one the technical and the other the meritorious one. Why does he mix them up?
' Mr. GRAHAM. I have dealt with the meritorious one; now I am dealing with the other. On the meritorious one, I do not think he has any argument on his side at all. On the technical one, there is possibly a difference between legal gentlemen, but I have given the opinion of more than one legal man, including some of my hon. friend's own friends. I say again, if my hon. friend's argument be founded on good logic and good law, then his Bill is not necessary. But that he does not really place much confidence in his own statement of the law is evidenced by the fact that he brings in a Bill to protect the municipalities against a power which he says does not exist. Now, last year we agreed that railways in the future, knowing the Act as it has been placed on the statute-book, ought to be held responsible if the commissioners found that an evil existed. In the city of Ottawa, just a few weeks ago, although the municipality and the railway company did practically agree on a certain level crossing, the commission refused to allow the crossing to be made in the way proposed. It shows the trend of public opinion and the wish of the commission to compel railway companies in the future to be very careful about creating a dangerous condition by means of level crossings. I say that is not injurious to or a discrimination against railways. The railways that have been constructed under the old conditions are now being compelled to suit themselves to the new requirements, and as we have been a party, to a certain extent, to the old conditions, in having al-

lowed them to create those crossings, we are prepared to assist them to a small degree in removing them, but we give them notice that in the future, if they create such crossings, we shall not help them to remedy any evil that may exist in consequence. I do not think that is unfair to the railway companies or to the people. Should we allow this Bill to pass? I say no. We passed the Act of last year after a lot of consideration and debate. Both sides of the House spent hour after hour on it, and we got what we thought was a good Bill, and one which I think would not be improved, but would be injured, by this amendment. We should at least allow the Act which we passed last session to have a chance to go into operation before we begin tinkering with it in one direction or another. Make this amendment this session, and next session we shall have amendments asking for a relief in some contrary direction. I believe that the Act passed last year, if we give it a fair trial, will remove in a measure at least the great evil that exists, and believing that to be the case, I cannot accept this Bill and must ask the House to vote down its second reading.

After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I overlooked a phase of the question when discussing the Bill before six o'clock. In hundreds of instances the railways were in possession before there was a highway. Under the old Railway Committee of the Privy Council, a very marked distinction was always made in regard to priority of occupation. In a case where a railway had run through a portion of country before a highway was constructed, that fact was always taken into consideration in a decision by the Railway Committee as to the method and apportionment of the cost of a crossing. In order to express what I wish to in reference to[ this Bill, I think the proper procedure would be for my motion to take the form that the Bill be not now read a second time, but be read this day six months, and I 'beg leave to move accordingly.

I would like the minister's opinion upon the case of a crossing which originally was a level crossing, but at which the railway, in order to reduce a grade, depressed the track by six or seven feet. In such a case would the municipality be called upon to pay their proportion of the cost of erecting an overhead bridge?

That would be a case for the Railway Commission and the facts my hon. friend has adduced would afford) a strong ground for the municipality to ask
exemption from contributing to the cost of such a bridge.

I do ,'not agree with the Minister of Railways that the conditions to-day are the same as the conditions at the time of which he spoke, years and years ago, when in their anxiety to secure railways the people of Canada were willing to allow them to run on the level of the highway and when many municipalities granted bonuses to secure railways within their borders. Those are by no means the conditions for which we have to legislate to-day. In those days every train stopped at every station and the fastest train did not run 25 miles an hour. The fatalities that occur to-day are caused by the fast through trains running 50 or 60 miles an hour that do not in any way serve the municipalities that are asked to bear the cost of protecting the lives of their people at these deadly level crossings. In the days of which the minister spoke there were no trains of this character, no train passed through a town or village at such a rate of speed that accidents could not easily be avoided at level crossings. There would not be the same objection to the expenditure of this money by the municipalities if the result would be to absolutely safeguard the lives of people within the municipalities by the entire elimination of level crossings. My Bill does not apply to the conditions mentioned by the minister. This Bill applies only so long as the trains continue to run on the King'S highway.
As to the hundreds of instances which the minister has just mentioned, I fancy that is a little bit of imagination too, when he says there were hundreds of cases where the railways were in possession before the highway was constructed. In some large cities new crossings have been opened up, and those are always dealt with as they arise, that is a matter of new construction. But in the great majority of cases where the trouble arises to-day, the highways existed before the railway was built, in villages and towns where the railway stopped, ail'd where they did not have the fast running trains we have to-day and which can hardly avoid killing people. To corroborate that statement you have only to look at the statistics, and you will find that in every case where these accidents have happened, they have occurred by trains running fifty or sixty miles an hour through villages and towns where they did not stop.

Mr. NORTHRUP moved the seoond read-inf of Bill (No. 5) to amend the Railway Act.

I think this is the same Bill that received the attention of the House some few years ago and was rejected. It was on the Order Paper last year, but, if I remember correctly, it was not reached. This Bill proposes an amendment to the present Railway Act, not so much, as I understand, to meet general cases as to meet a specific case. I do not care to go into the details as the House has heard the argument time and again from the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) as to a contract that was made some years ago between the railway company in the county of Hastings which he contends was never carried out by the company. Instead, the railway was transferred to another company. If I remember my hon. friend correctly, speaking last year, he said that a certain amount of money, paid by the late Conservative government, was caused to be paid through error and accepted fraudulently by the company. This Bill, if I understand it, is intended to be retroactive, to give the commission power to deal with the whole matter which had its

origin nineteen or twenty years ago. The matter was thoroughly discussed on a previous occasion. I do not care to detain the House, but I do not think that the government can see its way clear to accept the Bill, and as sending it to the committee will only be postponing the evil day, I beg to .move in amendment that the Bill be not [DOT] now read the second time but that it be read the second time this day six months.

Mr. Speaker, the only regret I have is that this Bill, which I have introduced, will not come into operation within the next few months because it certainly must come into .operation after the next session of this House for there is no other point to which the minister can move but that one, he having been on every side of the compass with that exception. The minister objects to this Bill on what he regards as sufficient grounds. The first ground is that the Bill has already been rejected by this House. If this Bill had been rejected by the House that might be an argument, though certainly not a conclusive argument, against the present motion but, unfortunately, the minister is wrong. I am obliged, speaking in the parliamentary sense, to accept his statement, but I can assure you that it was the greatest surprise of my life to learn that this Bill had been rejected by this House, because it certainly was not my Bill, it was not during the time I was in the House that the Bill was rejected and therefore I cannot help having some kind of suspicion that the minister, when he gave that as a reason for not allowing this Bill to pass, was not stating the reason that was, at all events, uppermost in his mind. Then there was another reason, and that was that this Bill was introduced to meet a particular case. The minister is just as accurate in that statement as he was in the preceding one and not one bit more so. But it does seem rather an insult to a member of this House, when he introduces a Bill that he believes to be in the interests of the country, that a minister will deliberately oppose that Bill and give two reasons for the throwing out of that Bill on the strength of which two reasons there is not the slightest doubt in the world that this intelligent "body will throw that Bill out, and yet there is not the slightest shadow of a ground of excuse for either of the reasons he gave. One would hardly believe it possible that there could be such ingratitude in this world. I remember a time, only a couple of years ago, when this very same matter was brought by myself before the House, and at that time the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals, the same gentleman who to-day fills the position and moves so sensibly and on such meritorious .grounds that this Bill should be thrown out, almost with 16
tears in his eyes, regretted the lamentable state of .affairs that existed and declared that he was looking for a remedy therefor. Let me tell the House what the minister thought of this same Bill two or three years ago when the Bill was first brought in and when, whatever may have occurred since, there had been no opportunity for any railway corporation to influence, the minister or express its opinion in regard to this Bill. In those early days, when perhaps the minister's conscience was more sensitive, as he had been in office but a short time, speaking of this very measure, the minister thus expressed himself. I had laid before the House the grounds upon which I complained that the people of this country were suffering .a grievance. The minister says that it is not necessary to repeat all the details, and I will not weary the House by repeating the full details of the story I told, but the .story I told was of the manner in which this country had been robbed of $21,000 .by a railway .corporation, and after I had pointed out that the case was not met by existing law and asked if there was no remedy, the minister spoke of this lamentable state of affairs and said:
We are anxious to find a remedy so that this will not occur again. The people have a grievance not only on account of the subsidies voted by this House, but on account of the votes by municipalities throughout Ontario and in other jn-ovinces. . . There is a weakness in the law somewhere that ought to be remedied, and I assure the House that I am trying to find out the method to remedy this grievance. If possible I shall have something further to say a little later on so that the Railway Commission or some authority may be given power to deal with such cases and compel companies to carry out their contracts with the people of Canada. . . I will say further that I will not be satisfied until I do find some way. I do not believe that a railway company lias a right to take the money of the people of Canada and then not carry out its contract any more than it would have a right to take my money and not carry out a contract entered into with me.
That was not this Minister oi Railways.

'Twas he. As I said a few moments ago about another matter, does it not almost seem to be .a farce for hon. members of this House to waste their time preparing legislation in order to assist a minister to relieve himself of anxiety that is wearing him out and bringing him perhaps to an early grave through worry? And, when I found a reme'dy for him last year, the House did not reject the Bill but when it came up the first time it could not be moved because it had not been printed in both languages, and another unfortunate Bill was ahead of it-whether it was that Bill the government did not wish to



have read or my Bill I know not-but at all events no further opportunity of calling the attention of the House to the merits of this Bill was given. So Sir, I say that practically at the request of the Minister of of Railways I introduce this measure, because, when he informed this House that there was a grievance, that this grievance ought to be reme'died and that he would not rest until he had found a remedy, I felt I was conferring a favour on the hon. gentleman when, in discharging my duty to my constituents and the people of this country I offered him a remedy which he himself was not able to discover. If we find the minister speaking the truth, as of course he did speak the truth when he admitted there was a grievance; if we find the minister speaking the truth in all conscientiousness which of course he did when he said he desired to find a remedy; and if we find him speaking the truth, as I admit he did when he declared he would not rest until he found a remedy, then when the remedy is offered and the minister declines to accept it, what are we to think? This House has heard the objections made to the present measure but not one word dropped from the lips of the minister to show that the Bill [DOT]did not meet the desire of his heart to furnish him with the remedy he sought. But, merely, because, first, it had been rejected which it had not, and secondly, because it is to meet an isolated case which it is not, he asked the House to reject the Bill. The minister can hardly be surprised to find that I and other members of this House have their strong suspicions that there is some other reason actuating the minister, than the two most unfounded reasons which he has given to the House. Now Sir, what other reasons can possibly exist? The minister says this is an isolated case and therefore, possibly because I happen to sit on the opposite of the House from him, he thinks my constituents are not entitled to redress. But there sits on my left the member for Missisquoi (Mr. Meigs) a more faithful supporter of the government than whom does not sit in this House and he requested me to push the Bill because in his constituency there are some cases precisely similar to the one in my own constituency. An hon. gentleman sits behind the minister, the gentleman from the county of Perth who, whether or not he himself is aware of the fact, his predecessor was aware of it and was prepared to assist me in carrying this Bill because in the county of Perth there arc illustrations precisely similar to the one in the county of Hastings. Other members of this House have in their own constituencies precisely similar conditions, and therefore when the minister objects to this legislation on the ground that it is only to meet an isolated ease there is no Mr. NORTHRUP
more reason for that excuse than there is for the others he gave. Is it possible that in the parliament of Canada in the twentieth century a minister would dare occupy a seat in this House, and without denying the facts in this case refuse to remedy the grievance? These facts are that the Crown had been robbed of $21,000 by a railway company which made an application for it to the Crown under the name of another company which did not exist; that it obtained a cheque from the government payable to the order of a railway company that ha'd ceased to exist years before; that it endorsed that cheque in the name of a company which had no longer any existence and deposited that cheque to its own credit in the bank and was wrongfully the beneficiary of over $21,000 of the money of the people of this country; that a contract was entered into in the name of a non-existant company by one of the great corporations of Canada to-day; that that contract expressly recited and agreed that the recipient of the money, the bogus nonexisting company was to continuously and perpetually operate this line of railway seven miles only in length, would it be believed that in the face of these facts and when it is pointed out that unfortunately under the wording of the Railway Act no relief lies at present, because that great corporation if it was brought into court would say that it did not make the contract and that the company that did make the contract does not exist, any more than it did when the money was paid over in its name; would it be believed that when under these circumstances I ask the government to 'do something to recover for the people of this country the $21,000 which have been most improperly taken from their pockets, the minister while admitting this state of affairs, while regretting the scandal that the law should be as it is, while declaring in this House that he deplored that state of affairs and never would rest until he found a remedy, now deliberately stands before this House and refuses to accept the remedy which is offered to him, and refuses on grounds which I 'do not think he would venture to state before me on a public platform in the county of Hastings where I could use language that the rules of this House unhappily prevent me from using here. Now, it has been said by the minister that this legislation is only to meet a state of affairs that arose in the past, that it is ex post facto legislation. Why, Sir, when the very board to which I wish to appeal was created, was there a single solitary shred of jurisdiction given to that Railway Board which did not stand on exactly the same footing that this case stands on which I to-day wish to bring before the board.
They are dealing with retroactive matters all the time.

Certainly, they all stand on the same footing. There was no Railway Board until the Act created it and gave it jurisdiction to deal with matters that had occurred up to that time as well as with matters that might occur in the future. And when, unhappily, it was found from time to time, as it has been found in many cases, that the Act constituting the Railway Board unfortunately did not go far enough and that a grievance had arisen for which there was no remedy, the government itself, led by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, has come to ihis House again and again and again and amended the Railway Act to give to the Railway Commissioners the power that they thought was necessary to do justice to the people of this country. And, when to-day, I ask him to do precisely what has been done again and again and again; when I ask him to give to the board power

not to compel them to take any steps but merely to give jurisdiction to the board-that when certain facts are brought before them, the fact that the people have been deprived of their money and the contract not carried out, that the board may have jurisdiction to make such orders as may seem reasonable in the premises. I do not even provide that if the matter is brought before the board they must make any particular order. I merely ask that in such a case the board may give such an order as is reasonable in the premises. The hon. minister has so little confidence in his own board, or so little confidence in the honesty of the people he is defending, that he is not willing to allow this matter to come before the board and give them jurisdiction to make such an order as they may think reasonable and fair. Now, I would like the minister to be honest in this respect and to tell me which it is he distrusts: the honesty of those-I can hardly call them his clients -the honesty of those recipients of the $21,000 whom he is protecting, or the integrity of the broad which he will not trust with such a matter as this. There is no escape from the dilemma. The hon. gentleman admits the grievance. He has declared it publicly on the floor of this House and therefore he cannot deny it. He has declared that a grievance existed and he wished to find a remedy for it, and now when a remedy is offered he Tefuses to accept it.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me? He has repeated that so often that he may possibly come himself to believe that it is founded on fact. If he will just read carefully the wording of my 16i
language which he himself has read, he will see that my observations were addressed to a remedy for future cases which might arise.
He had described this case as he has to-night, only at more length. I fear the hon. gentleman is not quoting exactly what I said, but if the hon. gentleman consults 'Hansard5, he will find that at that time there was a division taken and that my contention was upheld on practically the same Bill which he has before the House to-night. I was speaking in general terms and for the future, while my hon. friend tries to make out that 1 was discussing his own case.

I do not wish to have any question of veracity between the hon. gentleman and myself. I asked a question in the House the other day as to the accuracy of these words, which were taken from 'Hansard5, copied by myself; and even at the risk of being charged by the hon. gentleman with repeating the words once more, I will read from 'Hansard5 exactly what he said. While the hon. gentleman the other day, in answering my question, said very astutely that the sentences were taken from different j^arts of his speech, which was perfecly true, yet it is also true that there is in the context, not one word to modify the statement made by the hon. gentleman at that time. In fact, so eloquent and convincing was the hon. gentleman that his leader assented, and said there was a grievance that should be remedied. Therefore I thought the remedy was at hand. That there may be no doubt as to what the hon. gentleman did say, I will read his exact words, as found in 'Hansard5 'of 1907-8, at pages 2815 and 2816:
We are anxious to find a remedy so that this will not occur again. The people have a grievance not only on account of the subsidies voted by this House, but on account of the votes by municipalities throughout Ontario and in other provinces.
There is a weakness in the law somewhere that ought to be remedied, and I assure the House that I am trying to find out the method to remedy this grievance.
1 will say further that I will not be satisfied until I do find some way. I do not believe a company has a right to take the money of the people of Canada and then not carry out its contract any more than it would have a right to take my money and not carry out a contract entered into with me.
Does the hon. gentleman think to night that a railway company has the right to use the name .of a non-existing railway company to obtain( $21,000 of the money of the people of Canada, to execute a contract in the name of a non-existing railway company, to get the money, to endorse a cheque in the name of a non-existing railway company, and deposit it in a

bank to its own credit, and then decline to carry out one of the conditions under which the money was paid? Does the hon. gentleman think that he and his colleagues have no responsibility to the .people of Canada in a case of this kind? Has the day come when the principle can be laid down, probably to be quoted as a precedent in other cases, that if once money can be filched from the public treasury and be placed in the pocket of any one not entitled to it, although you may prove that the money was improperly obtained, and although you may show the very pocket in which it still rests, nothing can be done by this House, because the muney Having beeii obtained, it would not be fair to pass ex post facto legislation, and make the recipient pay the money back, but we will see that in future no one catches us in the same way? Is that to be the highest type of political foresight that we are to find in this House? Now, I do not wish to occupy the time of the House, because I assume that, the government having committed themselves against the Bill, it will not pass. I am perfectly willing, if they insist,^ that the Bill will be thrown out, on a division without taking time to call in the members and have the vote recorded-but at all events, I will insist on this, that it the Bill is not accepted by the government every year that I occupy a seat in "Hs Hcmse, i will make them vote as they did last year, and as they apparently intend vote to-night, that it is not right to give the Railway Commission an opportunity to mi?-? railway company pay back money ^ ls admitted it improperly received. . e government and their supporters are satisfied with this public exhibition of the ideas entertained by this government of the standard of right and wrong that should prevail with regard to the handling of public funds I can only hope that the day is not far distant when the people of this country, estimating these hon. gentlemen at their true value, will place in office gentlemen from this side of the House who, whatever their faults, will not fail in this respect, but null be prepared to stand up not for the rights of a defaulting corporation but for the rights of the people of this country.

speechtext: What railways is the hon. minister talking about as having been fused at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The various amalgamations as detailed in the debates of the House the session before last. There were several pieces of legislation which the hon. gentleman himself narrated and which appear in ' Hansard.' If I recollect correctly, the Belleville and North Hastings Railway Company was originally fused with the Grand Junction Company. Thus a company was formed which fused with the Midland railway. Then immediately afterwards that new company was fused with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. So just as the first two fused companies represented both the Belleville and North Hastings Company and the Grand Junction Company, the new company formed when the Midland was fused with that first one, represented the three companies which had gone into the amalgamation together, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which existed after the final piece of legislation, represented all four. The provincial legislature was careful, by the Acts which effected these; fusions to provide that the liabilities, debts and obligations of each of the companies, dealt with and formed into one, were to be carried on as liabilities, debts' and obligations of the new cmpany. Therefore I am quite unable to understand on what principle it is my hon. friend continually represents the company which had earned this subsidy as one which had no existence at the time the money was paid it. I would have thought that my hon. friend, as a lawyer, if he had been advising the government of 1888 and had been told by that government that there was a certain railway company which had earned its subsidy and was entitled to the money, but that the government were a little uncertain how they should make out the cheque for that subsidy and wanted his advice-I would have thought that he would have advised the government to make their check payable to the company with which they had a contract and which had done the work and earned the money and presented its certificate showing that it was
entitled to be paid. My hon. friend says that the,payment was a fraud on the public, that the money was filched from the treasury. All I can say is that the company to which the cheque was payable received the money, as shown by its endorsement of the cheque, I am speaking of facts which my hon. friend himself put before the House the session before last. The cheque shows the endorsement by the payees, the properly constituted officials of this very company, but the endorsement upon the cheque was for deposit to the credit of the Grand Trunk railway, and my hon. friend says that makes it all wrong. I remember two years ago asking my hon friend to explain what would have been the difference if this company, having earned the money, had, instead, of a cheque, received the money in current coin of the realm and handed that coin over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and I have never heard any explanation of what wrong there would have been in that. The money was earned, the company had complied with the conditions of the statute governing the subsidy, there was nothing in the statute about operating the railway, and I am unable to see what difference it would make whether the company paid the money to the Grand Trunk railway or deposited it in the bank to its own; credit or threw it into* Lake Ontario.
My hon. friend says there has been great wrong done the people of his county because that line has not been operated during the last twenty-one years, and he presented that circumstance as a grievance when addressing the House on the subject two years ago. The Minister of Railways then told the House that if a repetition of such a state of things, as my hon. friend from Hastings had described, could be prevented, if there was any way of preventing it, he would take that way. The extracts which the hon. gentleman made from the remarks on that date of the Minister of( Railways, as pointed out in the answer given the other day to the interrogatories on the subject, were not continuous extracts. Sentences between were omitted and the quotations which the hon. gentleman put into the question he framed, were not given in the order of the sentences as uttered by the Minister of Railways. I venture to say that any one who reads the speech of the minister, as reported in ' Hansard,' will plainly see that every reference he made in that case was not to the individual grievance of which my hon. friend from Hastings was speaking but to the general question, and that he was pledging himself to the House upon that occasion that he would take the earliest means in his power to put on our statute-book, if he could find it, some remedy that would prevent any repetition of such circumstances

The pages to which the hon. gentleman has referred are incorrectly given in the citation from which he was just reading. They are correctly given in the answer to the question of the hon. minister a week or ten days ago, as 2815 and 2816 of ' Hansard,' 1907-8 in the report of the proceedings of February 10, 1908. What followed? During the course of that session the Minister of Railways thought he had succeeded in finding a remedy and he prepared and presented to this House his Bill amending the Railway Act, empowering the Board of Railway Commissioners to consider any future case of this character which should arise and conferring upon that board a new power by giving to any person entitled to apply to that board the new remedy of compelling all railway companies specifically to carry out every obligation into which they had entered. That was a vast step in advance in the legal history of this country. Up to that time, a railway company which might have entered into a contract that it would maintain a station, that it would operate a road or that it would do some other continuous piece of work, enjoyed this position of advantage not peculiar to a railway company, but which would apply and would exist in favour of any similar organization; the courts which have the power to compel people to,, carry out their contracts specifically have for a long series of years both in this country and in England, refused to pronounce any decree which the officers of those courts would not be in a position to see enforced. They had refused to pronounce a decree which would in terms order a railway company, for instance, to operate its road. How was such a decree to be enforced? It would need the sheriff or some other officer of the court to stand day by day through week after week or month after month over the company to see that it complied with the order of the court and because it was a task of that continuous character, which would involve the taking control of the railway and administering its affairs, the courts had long refused to pronounce any such decree, or judgment of that character as against a railway company or any other company which might have entered into such a contract. Under this legislation, which the Minister of Railways introduced and carried through the House during the session before last, the Board of Railway Commissioners is given precisely that power and for the first time in the history of this Dominion a court has been specifically empowered to take hol'd of a railway company, and compel it to live up to its obligations and to carry out specifically any contract of this character into which it may have entered.
When that legislation was under consideration in this House my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) was not satisfied with it, he Mr. AYLESWORTH.
thought it would not cover this particular case which lay so near his heart and he urged that its language should be so widened that it would not merely include and cover cases which might arise in the future and which the hon. minister, by his Bill, was seeking to, guard against; but that the legislation should be so worded that it would cover this old outlawed claim of his of twenty odd years ago. He' pressed that upon the House, the matter was fully discussed in Committee of the Whole House, the committee was against him but he was not content. On the motion for the third reading of the Bill he proposed by way of amendment that there should be added to the Bill a clause in the very words, word for word and line for line, of this Bill now printed and now under the consideration of the House. He pressed his argument to the utmost and after a full discussion divided the House and on June 30, 1908, by a vote of 77 against 36, the House declined to accept the amendment of the hon. gentleman and accepted instead the Bill as framed by the Minister of Railways. My hon. friend is not content with that. He brings this Bill before the House and seeks to insist that it must be passed and that this duty which in 1908, only eighteen months ago, this House declined to put upon the Railway Board, should now be added to it.
We must in fairness to the hon. gentleman's Bill meet it not with reference to the particular facts of the special case which he described but with reference to its provisions and we must see in what way it would change the existing law. The existing law is to be found in the amending or substituted section of last session. On May 19 last the Royal Assent was given to the Bill of last session which empowers the Railway Board to deal in the way the hon. gentleman desires with all future cases of this character and the one point of substantial difference-there are verbal differences but they are matters of detail-between the Act as it now stands upon our statute-book and the Bill now under consideration is to be found in lines 21 and 22, and in lines 31 and 32 of the present Bill. That is simply a provision including the obligations of either the contracting company or any person or corporation which has acquired or owns or is in possession or occupation of or is operating the railway. Bear in mind that the present law imposes this obligation to carry out its contract to the full upon the contracting party but that will not suit the case of my hon. friend. He wants Paul to pay Peter's debt. He is not content with the present law which would make the company which contracted to do a certain thing do that thing, but he wants to make some other company do it and accordingly he frames this Bill to cover not only the case of the company which enters

into the contract but, in terms, to extend to and cover the case of any person or corporation which has acquired or owns, or is in possession or occupation of or is operating the railway. Now is that right? Ought that to be the law? If I buy a house and there is a mortgage on that house, I know that I must pay that mortgage before I can own that house free of encumbrance. But when I buy a house which is free of encumbrance, I hope I do not undertake to pay the coal bill of the former owner, I hope that I am not entering upon an obligation to pay any and all of the debts which the man who sold that house to me has contracted. And yet, that is identically and exactly the principle which my hon. friend wants to incorporate into this Bill now before the House and to enforce against the company which has purchased the property of the company that he says is in default. I think that principle needs only to be stated, needs only to be understood to justify every one in supporting the amendment which seeks to postpone for six months the consideration of this measure.
I,	Sir, am not prepared by any vote I give in this House to enable some person who has a debt against one man to collect that debt from another man simply because that other man may have come into possession of the property of the man who owes the debt. That, stating it in plain English, is the position which this Bill seeks to put any railway company, or other person, or company, in, if such railway company, or other person, or company, has acquired or is operating a railway line. It seems to me that such legislation is wrong in principle. That was the view in which the proposition of my hon. friend was opposed from this side of the House during the previous session. The matter was then very fully discussed and debated, the matter was then pressed to the ultimate extreme of dividing the House on the subject, and I for my part certainly see no reason whatever to depart from thg course which was taken then in rejecting the proposition of my hon. friend.

With regard to the last reason which the minister has given for his course to-day, in my judgment it does not hold good, because parliament has already done the same thing once or twice, or more, with regard to roads that had been purchased by other companies than the original owners. I can cite one or two instances where the labour was paid, and parliament compelled the new company to pay the cost of the labour that went into the construction of the road long before it was sold. We have done this several times in parliament. We did it with the old Northwest Central railway, we did it with the railway
extending south from Hamilton, and we have done it in one or two other instances, I think one in the province of Quebec many years ago. So there is more than one precedent for it; and the argument which the Minister of Justice addressed to the House as the strongest reason why it should not be done, has in my judgment very little force in it, because parliament has already done it.
